title: Quantum sensing could become the next foundation of navigation
key_facts: Nir Sharon, Chief Quantum Technology Scientist at Quantum X Labs and an associate professor of applied mathematics at Tel Aviv University, argues GPS has a weakness because its signal can be blocked or spoofed with little effort.
He says dead reckoning (estimating position from a known start by measuring direction and movement) suffers from errors that build up with every movement.
He argues quantum gyroscopes and miniaturised atomic clocks could reduce that build-up so machines keep useful positioning when satellites are unavailable.
Quantum X Labs is an Israeli company working on quantum computing, software and sensing; its sensing products include a quantum gyroscope and a miniaturised rubidium atomic-beam clock.
According to Sharon the company has scientific prototypes and proof-of-concept systems in laboratories, and is working with partners to move toward products.
He describes the present challenge as increasingly engineering: making the sensors compact, robust and suited to specific industries.
The article gives no test results, performance figures or product dates.
quote_evidence: “The problem with GPS is almost the success of GPS itself,” Sharon explains.
According to Sharon, the company has scientific prototypes and proof-of-concept systems operating in laboratory environments, with work underway to translate them toward product applications.
why_it_matters_hint: GPS can be jammed or faked, so navigation that does not depend on satellites is attractive for autonomous vehicles and defence, but this is a company view with lab prototypes only.
